title: Foundation for Virtual and Augmented Reality Systems

lectures.title: Interactive System Development Life Cycle Stages

course_goals.text: Analyze the fundamental concepts, history, and scope of Extended Reality (XR) systems by defining the reality-virtuality continuum and classifying various XR technologies.
Evaluate the impact of human factors and sensory perception on immersive experience, including analyzing biological limitations, the causes of cybersickness, and the role of multi-sensory design.
Design and implement user-centered interactive systems by applying principles of usability, interaction design, and complex locomotion techniques.
Engineer XR applications by mastering the architecture of modern hardware, advanced tracking methodologies, and the computer graphics rendering pipeline.
Validate, optimize, and deploy XR systems by conducting rigorous empirical evaluations, applying system optimization algorithms, and utilizing professional development tools.

concepts.definition: Task execution is a structured process organized into a beginning part, a middle part, and an end part to ensure the user understands the working and how to proceed.
concepts.reason: a single key term

facets.says: Task execution should be structured into clear beginning, middle, and end parts, and feedback must be provided for each group.

concepts.name: Subtask
concepts.definition: Subtasks are the many smaller tasks that comprise a larger activity and can be organized into a beginning, middle, and end structure.
concepts.reason: a single key term

facets.says: Subtasks are smaller components of a large activity, such as choosing items or payment in online shopping, and should be organized by structure.

concepts.name: Error prevention
concepts.definition: Error prevention is a design practice and characteristic where the interface is designed to help the user actively avoid making mistakes. It aims to minimize the possibility of errors and keep error rates low, such as by ensuring that "Close" and "Start" options are not kept close to each other.
concepts.reason: Both lecture entries describe the same design principle of minimizing user mistakes through interface layout and characteristics.

facets.says: To prevent errors, designers must arrange interface elements carefully, for instance, ensuring Start and Close options are not placed near each other.
Error prevention is a design characteristic where the interface actively guides the user to avoid making mistakes.

concepts.name: Easy reversal of action
concepts.definition: Easy reversal of action is a design objective that permits users to rectify mistakes or return from an erroneous situation. It is achieved by providing facilities such as undo and redo, and ideally, the reversal option should be kept available so that users can come back from an error.
concepts.reason: Both entries describe the same design objective of allowing users to rectify mistakes, with one phrasing emphasizing the ease of the process and the other identifying specific facilities like undo and redo.

facets.says: Easy reversal of action is a design objective, allowing users to recover from errors using standard facilities like undo and redo.

concepts.name: Keeping the user in control
concepts.definition: Keeping the user in control is a design goal that ensures users feel a sense of agency over the system, preventing them from feeling lost or overwhelmed by technical complexity.
concepts.reason: a single key term

facets.says: Keeping users in control is vital, especially for laypersons, to prevent them from feeling overwhelmed by technical complexity.

concepts.name: Change in system state
concepts.definition: Change in system state is the realization that something is happening within a system, which must be perceivable by the user.
concepts.reason: This entry stands alone as it describes the transition or event of something happening, which is a different concept from the state itself.

facets.says: The system must be designed so the user can perceive when something is happening, indicating a change in the system state.
A change in system state occurs when the user issues a command that alters the system's current state or mode.

concepts.name: Drag and drop operation
concepts.definition: A drag and drop operation is a method where the user visually perceives an object being moved from one area of an application to another and sees it placed in the desired location.
concepts.reason: This entry describes a specific method for moving objects within an application interface, which is distinct from navigation techniques.

facets.says: Operations like drag and drop require clear visual feedback, showing the user the object moving and being placed in the intended location.

concepts.name: Short term memory load
concepts.definition: Short term memory load is a design rule that involves minimizing the amount of information a user must remember by keeping the required chunks between 5 and 9.
concepts.reason: a single key term

concepts.name: Short-term memory
concepts.definition: Short-term memory is a component of memory that functions like a temporary notebook or non-permanent storage for holding immediate information while performing daily activities.
concepts.reason: This entry describes a distinct type of memory focused on temporary storage, which the lecturer distinguishes from long-term memory.

facets.says: Short-term memory acts as a temporary notebook for daily tasks, ideally limiting information load to between 5 and 9 chunks.

concepts.name: 7 plus or minus 2 rule
concepts.definition: The 7 plus or minus 2 rule, originally proposed by George Miller, suggests that the optimal capacity for information held in short term memory is between 7 to 9 chunks.
concepts.reason: a single key term

facets.says: George Miller's rule states that the optimal capacity for short-term memory is maintained when keeping between 7 to 9 chunks of information.

concepts.name: Chunk of information
concepts.definition: A chunk of information is essentially a defined unit of information that can represent anything from a single letter or word to an entire sentence or concept, and its size varies by application.
concepts.reason: a single key term

facets.says: A chunk of information is a flexible unit of data that can represent anything from a single letter to an entire concept, depending on the application.

concepts.name: Object interaction
concepts.definition: Object interaction is a type of interaction used in immersive settings where users select and manipulate objects that are part of the virtual environment.
concepts.reason: This entry stands alone as it defines a broad category of interaction that encompasses both selection and manipulation.

concepts.name: Navigation
concepts.definition: Navigation is an interaction type in immersive environments—distinct from object interaction and system control—that describes the process of moving a user from one point to another within a virtual world, which necessitates a change in the user's viewpoint or field of view. In a VR setting, it is quantified by the duration or distance covered and is designed to minimize cyber sickness.

Navigation is the process of moving between points in the virtual world, which requires a corresponding change in viewpoint.
The goal of navigation is defined as changing the user's field of view or viewpoint by moving the user from one point to another.
Navigation consists of two components: Locomotion (the motor component) and the second component, which is Wayfinding.
Efficient movement and navigation within a complex environment are impossible without suitable wayfinding support.
Navigation interaction comprises travel and wayfinding.
Navigation features were specifically integrated into the Majuli tour to suit the different categories of users.
The virtual tablet acts as the main interface and provides the navigation tools.

Navigation is the key area of optimization, requiring strategies that minimize cyber sickness by controlling either the distance or the duration of movement.

Navigation duration can be adjusted by controlling virtual travel speed or modifying the terrain and world size.

Navigation optimization involves two approaches: finding the minimum time path, or maximizing POIs within a time constraint.
Users resume navigation after stopping at a point of interest to inspect or interact with it.
Navigation techniques are applied specifically: walking for movement within a point, and other methods across points.

concepts.name: Interaction for system control
concepts.definition: Interaction for system control is a regular type of interaction in immersive environments used to manage system-related settings, initialize parameters, and provide initial information such as menus and options. concepts.reason: The lecturer uses 'system control' and 'interaction for system control' interchangeably to describe the third broad category of interaction in immersive environments, distinct from object interaction and navigation.

Interaction for system control is used to set up the system, initialize parameters, and manage options or menus.
System control is the third category of interaction, relying on familiar techniques used in any standard computer system.
System control interaction is used to issue commands, change system state, or mode, similar to standard operations in any software.

concepts.name: Selection
concepts.definition: Selection is the act of specifying or choosing one or more objects from a defined set of virtual objects within the virtual world.

Selection is categorized as one of the four broad categories utilized for locomotion in the virtual world.
Selection is listed as a specific type of object interaction that occurs within the virtual world environment.
Selection is identified as a fundamental interaction capability in the Scene View, allowing developers to choose game objects.

concepts.name: Object manipulation
concepts.definition: Object manipulation is an interaction technique performed after selection that allows a user to change the properties of a virtual object, such as its position or orientation, often through hand manipulation.
concepts.reason: These entries refer to the same specific interaction technique where an object's properties are modified after it has been selected.

facets.says: Manipulation occurs after selection and involves changing the properties of the selected virtual object.
Object manipulation involves changing properties (like position or color) after selection, using techniques like hand, indirect, or bimanual methods.

concepts.name: Target occlusion
concepts.definition: Target occlusion is a situation where a target object is partially or completely hidden from view by other surrounding objects, making selection a challenging task.
concepts.reason: a single key term

facets.says: Target occlusion impacts selection performance, and for fully occluded objects, the user must be made aware of their presence.

concepts.name: Hand selection technique
concepts.definition: Hand selection technique is a method that utilizes the user's physical hand to select objects within a virtual world.
concepts.reason: These entries use different names to describe the same concept of using a physical hand to select objects in a virtual world.

facets.says: This technique utilizes the physical user's hand or handheld devices to perform object selection within the virtual environment.

concepts.name: Virtual hand
concepts.definition: A virtual hand is an avatar of the user's physical hand that is visible in the virtual world and tied to the user's actual physical motion. It serves as a selection technique that provides a one-to-one mapping of the physical hand to manipulate objects.
concepts.reason: All descriptions for E1 describe the same avatar-based interaction tool used for selection and manipulation.

The virtual hand idea is extended to manipulate objects.

concepts.name: Tracked hand motion using tracked controllers
concepts.definition: Tracked hand motion using tracked controllers is a technique that ensures a virtual hand moves in a virtual world with exactly the same movements as the physical hand in the real world, providing a one-to-one mapping.
concepts.reason: This entry stands alone as it describes the specific technique and behavior of one-to-one movement mapping between physical and virtual hands.

facets.says: This technique uses 3D tracked controllers to maintain an exact, intuitive one-to-one mapping between the physical and virtual hand movements.

concepts.name: 3D tracked controller
concepts.definition: A 3D tracked controller is a type of hardware device typically used to implement a virtual hand that maintains a one-to-one mapping with the physical hand.
concepts.reason: This entry stands alone because it identifies the specific hardware device used to implement one-to-one tracked hand motion.

facets.says: 3D tracked controllers are used to implement the virtual hand, allowing for a direct, one-to-one mapping to the user's real hand.

concepts.name: Go-go technique
concepts.definition: The go-go technique is a method that allows the user to select distant objects without feeling tired by mapping smaller real hand movements to larger virtual hand movements. It functions by interactively changing the length of the virtual arm as the distance to the object increases.
concepts.reason: This entry describes a specific method for selecting distant objects by adjusting virtual arm length.

facets.says: The go-go technique allows users to change virtual arm length, mapping smaller real hand movements to larger virtual movements with higher speeds as distance increases to reduce fatigue.
Go-go technique is listed as one of the manipulation techniques used to implement manipulation-based locomotion.

concepts.name: Prism
concepts.definition: Prism is an improved selection technique that applies a scaled-down motion to the virtual hand when the user's hand movement speed is below a specified threshold.
concepts.reason: a single key term

facets.says: Prism is an improvement of the go-go technique that applies scaled-down motion to the virtual hand when the user's hand velocity is below a specified minimum.

concepts.name: Intent-driven selection
concepts.definition: Intent-driven selection is a technique where the user uses specific gestures or the posture of their virtual fingers to signal their level of confidence and intention to select an object, rather than simply moving the hand to it.
concepts.reason: a single key term

facets.says: Intent-driven selection uses specific virtual finger postures or gestures to indicate confidence and intention before selecting an object.

concepts.name: Proximity sphere
concepts.definition: A proximity sphere is a system employed in intent-driven selection that progressively refines object selection by changing size. It starts as a large sphere encompassing multiple objects and shrinks as the user moves closer to the intended object.
concepts.reason: a single key term

facets.says: Proximity spheres progressively reduce in size as the user moves closer to the intended object, refining the selection among surrounding items.

concepts.name: Travel technique
concepts.definition: A travel technique is a type of hand selection method that relies on physically moving the hand to select or locate an object. Examples of travel techniques include the go-go and prism methods.
concepts.reason: This entry describes a general category of selection methods, of which the go-go technique is a specific type.

facets.says: Travel techniques involve physically moving the hand to select or locate an object, contrasting with grabbing techniques like intent-driven selection.

concepts.name: Grabbing technique
concepts.definition: A grabbing technique is a type of hand selection method, such as intent-driven selection, that utilizes gestures or postures rather than continuous movement to achieve selection.
concepts.reason: This entry defines a general category of selection method and stands alone.

facets.says: Intent-driven selection is a grabbing technique where users use finger postures and gestures as an indication of confidence when selecting an object.

concepts.name: Pointing-based selection
concepts.definition: Pointing-based selection is a method where a user extends a ray into the virtual world to indicate that they want to select a particular object.
concepts.reason: This entry stands alone as it describes the general category of selection techniques involving the extension of a ray.

facets.says: It is a method where the user projects a ray into the virtual world to indicate their intent to select a specific object.

concepts.name: Hand pointing
concepts.definition: Hand pointing is a selection technique where the user points in the virtual world using their hand or handheld input devices, typically handheld devices. It can also involve using gaze pointing to estimate the target and trigger selection.
concepts.reason: This entry is a specific kind of pointing-based selection, making it a distinct concept from the general category.

facets.says: This is a selection technique where the user directs the ray using their physical hand or associated handheld input devices.

concepts.name: Head pointing
concepts.definition: Head pointing is a selection technique where the user moves their head in the virtual world to move a corresponding ray that extends from the head position into the distance. This allows for object selection without the use of a hand.
concepts.reason: This entry is a specific kind of pointing-based selection, making it a distinct concept from the general category.

facets.says: This technique uses head movement to move the ray from the head position, allowing object selection without requiring a physical hand.

concepts.name: Eye gaze pointing
concepts.definition: Eye gaze pointing is a selection technique where the user extends and changes the pointing ray using an eye tracker device to monitor their eye gaze.
concepts.reason: a single key term

facets.says: This technique uses eye tracking devices to monitor eye gaze, allowing the pointing ray to be controlled and changed by the user's gaze.

concepts.name: Ray casting
concepts.definition: Ray casting is a basic pointing-based selection technique where a user directs a virtual ray—represented as either a short line segment or an infinite line—into the environment to identify and intersect with a desired target. This method is used to indicate objects for selection, such as making selections on a start screen.
concepts.reason: These entries all describe the fundamental technique or method of using a virtual ray to point at and select objects in a virtual environment.

facets.says: This is the basic technique where a virtual ray is used to point at objects, typically representing a short or infinite line segment.
Ray casting is the foundational pointing idea that is extended by the use of a cone in volumetric selection.

concepts.name: Virtual ray
concepts.definition: A virtual ray is a short line segment or an infinite line that can be attached to the user's virtual hand, head, or eye depending on the input device used.
concepts.reason: E2 describes a distinct geometric representation used for interaction, separate from the avatar-based virtual hand.

facets.says: A virtual ray is a line segment or infinite line that can be attached to the virtual hand, head, or eye based on the input device.

concepts.name: Bend cast
concepts.definition: Bend cast is an improvement to ray casting where the system calculates point-line distance and bends the ray towards the selectable object closest to its path, reducing the need for precise pointing.
concepts.reason: a single key term

facets.says: Bend cast bends the virtual ray towards the object closest to the path by calculating point-line distances, reducing pointing precision.

concepts.name: Depth ray technique
concepts.definition: Depth ray technique is an improvement over basic ray casting used to resolve ambiguity when a pointing vector intersects multiple potential selection targets. It allows the system to pinpoint which specific object a user intends to select when a cast ray crosses multiple objects.
concepts.reason: This entry describes a specific improvement over basic ray casting to resolve selection ambiguity.

facets.says: This technique disambiguates targets when a pointing vector intersects multiple objects by selecting the one closest to the depth marker.

facets.says: The depth marker is an adjustable aid in depth ray technique that allows the user to indirectly indicate which object to select by controlling its position.

concepts.name: Image plane selection
concepts.definition: Image plane selection is a category of selection technique used in virtual worlds that selects objects based on a 2D view plane.
concepts.reason: This entry describes a selection technique based on a 2D view plane, making it a separate concept from volumetric selection.

facets.says: Image plane selection is a 2D technique where the user defines the view plane and uses hands or fingers to pinpoint the desired object.

concepts.name: Occlusion and framing

concepts.name: Volumetric selection
concepts.definition: Volumetric selection is a selection technique that enables a user to select a 3D region in virtual space, causing all corresponding objects within that region to be selected. concepts.name: Interaction technique
concepts.definition: Interaction technique is a method by which a user engages with an immersive experience. These techniques are broadly classified into three types: object interaction (which includes selection and manipulation interaction), navigation, and system control.
concepts.reason: This entry stands alone as it defines the overarching category of interaction methods.

facets.says: Immersive experiences incorporate specific techniques, such as selection, object manipulation, and various navigation methods.

concepts.name: Travel part
concepts.definition: The travel part is the motor component of navigation that refers to the actual movement of a user between two different locations or points in the virtual world. It is also known as locomotion, and the techniques used to let the user travel in a virtual world are called locomotion techniques or travel techniques.
concepts.reason: This entry is explicitly defined as a specific motor component or part of navigation rather than the general concept of navigation itself.

facets.says: The 'travel part' is the motor component of navigation, referring to the actual movement (locomotion) of the user between two locations.

concepts.name: Wayfinding
concepts.definition: Wayfinding is a component of navigation, distinct from locomotion or travel, that involves a mental model or cognitive process of the surroundings. It includes location awareness of where one is located and the ability to ascertain a path to a desired destination by transferring spatial knowledge to the real world. This process helps users build a mental map to locate themselves and identify suitable paths, which can be aided by miniature maps.
concepts.reason: Both entries describe wayfinding as one of the two components of navigation, with E1 using the phrase 'wayfinding part' and E2 providing the specific cognitive definitions for that component.

facets.says: Navigation consists of two components: locomotion (the motor component) and wayfinding.

Wayfinding is an essential requirement when designing complex virtual environments, supported by techniques like landmarks and miniature maps.

The ability to build a mental map is critical because it directly facilitates the user's success in performing wayfinding activities.

concepts.name: Exploration
concepts.definition: Exploration is a type of travel characterized by the lack of an explicit destination. The user moves around without a specific point to reach, instead wanting to see, learn, and observe things.

concepts.name: Walking-based locomotion

It is one of four broad types of locomotion, which also include steering-based, selection-based, and manipulation-based locomotion.

It allows users to focus on the desired destination rather than how to reach it, which differs from techniques that require continuous physical input for movement.

concepts.name: Partial gait technique
